# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

- Ingrid Haugen → author's invention: a gate No (writing up, no jobs that week).

- Claire Dubois-Martin → author's invention, filling a gap: a licensed binary with no source code, so the tested condition fails ('no').
- Hiroshi Takeda → [HN] "at least for everyone else, I'd would prefer tuning my own usage myself": he profiles a test run (Current solution mostly works; Adoption friction no).

- Diego Castañeda → [HN] the student's PDE simulation ("If I'm running a PDE simulation, and I allocate n machines I want to use all of them"); he keeps his margin (Adoption friction probably not).

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).
- Beatrix Okoro → [HN] "What you are really left with is the 'small and medium business' clusters that are purpose specific": a small cluster, less waste, a lower rung.
- Thomas Reinholt → [HN] the security objection ("a hard no"); would not pay.
- Leilani Kahale → [HN] "In many places the cost of the HPC hardware isn't passed onto them": a grant-funded university cluster that does not measure the waste (dont_know) and has no line for a monthly fee.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

insights_note: no grouping to read (no follow-up line with two answers)

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem to who asks and who gets a link, but the recency question (4) sits between two identical 'define exactly where this idea applies' screens (3 and 5), so the context step is split by a detour instead of finishing first.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the same kicker and question word for word ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'), so they read as the context being asked twice, unless each fills different fields, which the screen does not show. Screens 8 and 9 also ask the same event (a job failing mid-run or sitting on reserved compute) as reach and then frequency; that pairing is intended, not a repeat.
founder.missing: Nothing asks what a wrong guess costs a researcher: the days lost when a job is killed mid-run, the time spent waiting in the queue for an inflated request, or the share of reserved GPU hours left unused (my 30% to 59%). Screens 8 and 9 also bundle two different failures, under-requesting (the job dies) and over-requesting (the compute sits idle), into one count, so I cannot tell which one researchers actually feel. Screen 12 has a typo ('clusterr').

PRIMARY.order_why: It moves sensibly from whether I qualify, to how often I submitted, to my last run, and then to the resource guess for my last job, though the first two screens both say '1 of 4'.
PRIMARY.missing: Whether my last job was killed mid-run for under-requesting memory or time, and how much work and how many days I lost to it. Also what I actually requested compared with what the job really used, and whether I padded the request to avoid getting killed.

screens.why4: Using an AI face is a real choice, but the option is worded in Keel's product language rather than mine, and the hint does not say whether I could record myself or use a voice-only interviewer instead.
screens.why5: Nothing of my problem, roles or product is touched or leaked on this screen; it only sets the delivery.
screens.instead: Who should researchers see asking the questions? — Keel's AI interviewer (a face Keel picks, kept the same for everyone) / You, from a short video you record / No face, questions as text only

screens.why1: Once I've decided who asks, choosing how my researchers answer is the obvious next step before the link goes out.
screens.why2: The choice is clear, but 'Daphne Daphne' reads like a glitch and 'Still recording · ready in a few minutes' leaves me unsure whether something is recording me or the voice is still being built.
screens.why3: I know my researchers are at a desk between jobs and would rather tap than talk on video, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: Voice, text and letting them pick cover the real choices, they don't overlap, and each one says when it is ready.
screens.why5: It speaks of 'researchers', as I typed, and nothing about job sizes or clusters leaks into the format choice.
screens.instead: How should researchers answer? — AI interviewer: Daphne asks each question aloud on video, and every question is also on screen (her voice is ready in a few minutes) · Read and tap (ready now) · Let them choose (ready when Daphne is)

screens.why1: After choosing who asks and how researchers answer, the last thing to settle is who receives the link, so it belongs here at the end of the send step.
screens.why2: Plain to me as a founder sending a study, though each option's title runs into its description with no break ('People I know by name I send each one...'), which costs a half-second re-read.
screens.why3: I know who I'm reaching: researchers I know by name from the HPC and ML side, and I could equally post one open link in a cluster's user Slack or on HN.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel-built list and one open link posted where researchers already gather cover the real ways I would reach them, and each is distinct.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or my roles is reworded or leaked; the screen is only about distribution, and my pick of people I know by name is kept.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' is stated with 'Frequency: 4 answered' beside it, but the 5 needed sits only on the card, so the line does not say why 4 fails. It also names Frequency alone when Importance and Current solution are equally short.
screens.why_b2: Prevalence reads cleanly (6 of 7, bar 6 of 7, at the bar), but 7 people answered while the other three cards counted only 4, and nothing says why 3 dropped out, so I have to look twice to see what was counted.
screens.why_b3: Each card carries the dimension name and the belief line exactly as I checked it, including Importance and Current solution word for word.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do, such as sending the study to more researchers or how many more I need. The only closing text is a generic note on how the verdict is computed.
screens.why_b5: n is visible on every card, the short cards are called too few rather than read, and Prevalence holding at 6 of 7 is marked 'at the bar' rather than called strong.
screens.instead: Too few to call: Frequency, Importance and Current solution each counted 4 of the 7 who answered, and 5 are needed (3 were not counted because they had not submitted a job that week). Send it to a few more researchers who did submit before reading whether the problem holds.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 said yes against a bar of 6 of 7, so I know the belief held and the count that decided it.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows seven people on an axis of 0 to 7, six for and one against, and the marker at 6 is labelled as my bar of at least 8 in 10, so I get it on first look.
screens.why_b3: At least 8 in 10 researchers submitting a job in a working week is the prevalence I set, because everyone on a shared cluster submits, and it uses my words.
screens.why_b4: The So line hands me on to frequency and importance, but it does not tell me that at the bar exactly, one more no would have tipped it, or what that means for my segment.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 stays visible, the screen calls it a lean and not a call, and it says at your bar exactly rather than calling the result strong.
screens.instead: Holding up, but only just: 6 of 7 is exactly your bar, and one more no would drop it below, so treat submitting every week as likely, not settled, and read frequency next.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats '4 counted, 5 needed'.
screens.why_b2: The axis plainly counts working days out of 5 and gives the middle answer of 4, but I had to look twice at the bar: it reads '3 of 4 (at least 2 in 3)' while the strip has a fifth ghost cell and the screen says 5 are needed, and the legend shows a 'short of it' colour that no one is in.
screens.why_b3: 'Researchers try to submit a job on 3 to 5 working days out of 5' is the frequency I set myself, in my own words.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is a generic line: it does not tell me to get one more researcher's answer, and it does not tell me that all 4 counted are already inside my range.
screens.why_b5: The status line says '4 answered' when the count line says 6 answered and 4 counted, a soft misstatement of who replied, though 'a lean, not a call' keeps the small n honest.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of 6 counted, and all 4 submit on 3 to 5 days, with 5 needed; one more researcher's answer settles it, and even a No from them would still leave it holding at 4 of 5.

screens.why_b1: Too few to call sits right beside 4 answered and 5 needed to call it, so I know the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The bars count 8 picks from 4 people, but the strip shows 3 for and 5 against, which reads like 8 people; it takes a second look to see that the bar is 3 of 4 people.
screens.why_b3: The title Importance and the belief line are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing is settled here yet is generic; it does not say that one more counted researcher would decide it, or that 3 of 4 already clears my 2 in 3.
screens.why_b5: The low n is stated plainly, but the verdict says 4 answered while the count line says 6 answered, and the 3 for against 5 against strip makes a 3 of 4 lean look like a loss.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of the 4 researchers counted put guessing sizes in their two, above your 2 in 3, but 5 are needed; get one more clean answer, ideally from someone like Kwabena who sizes from past runs.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, 4 counted against 5 needed, so I know why there is no call.
screens.why_b2: The bands, my line and the marker at 3 of 4 are plain, but the verdict's '4 answered' clashes with the count line's '6 answered', and the single ghost cell beside two uncounted people takes a second look to see it means one more counted answer is needed.
screens.why_b3: The title 'Current solution' and the belief line are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't say that 3 of 4 already lean my way, or that one more counted answer would decide it.
screens.why_b5: Nothing is overclaimed and the small group is called a lean, but the headline '4 answered' understates the 6 who did answer, which is a soft misstatement of n.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 6 answered, 4 counted, and 3 of those 4 fell short (a lean your way); one more counted answer decides it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' is stated with '4 answered · 5 needed to call it' beside it, but the screen gives no tally of how many of the 4 put guessing in their two, so I cannot see which way it leans.
screens.why_b3: The Importance name and the belief line are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Too few to call implies I need more answers, but the screen never says to send the study to more researchers or how many more, and it says nothing about Current solution, which my belief also rested on.
screens.why_b5: The n of 4 and the single against stay visible, the verdict is withheld rather than overstated, and the one quote is shown as one person.
screens.why_b6: Kwabena's line, that sizes from last week's runs are fine and his day goes on data staging and library conflicts, names rival pains I did not type and a segment with history-based sizing that my pitch does not reach.
screens.instead: Say how the 4 split (e.g. 3 of 4 put guessing in their two) and tell me to send the study to at least 1 more researcher to call it, noting that the one against sizes from past runs and loses the day to data and software instead.

screens.why1: As the first screen it makes sense to check that I actually run jobs on a big cluster before asking anything else about my work.
screens.why2: "Run jobs on a cluster" and "GPUs" are exactly how I talk about my work, so I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know roughly how big our cluster is and whether I submit to it, though someone on a cluster near 100 GPUs might have to think for a second.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers a screener completely, and a gate rightly has no escape option.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but it drops "shared" and "SLURM or Kubernetes", so someone with a private 100-GPU box would pass even though the founder means shared clusters.
screens.why6: It is short and only one question, and "I'll read two options, yes or no" is easy to hold, if a little stiff for a yes-or-no question.
screens.instead: Do you submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes cluster with at least 100 GPUs? Yes; or No.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I'm on a big GPU cluster, asking whether I've submitted a job this week is the obvious next gate before asking for the story.
screens.why2: Submit a job is exactly how I talk about sbatch or kubectl apply, so I can answer on first read, though 'try to' made me wonder for a second if it means a submission that failed.
screens.why3: I submit jobs almost every day, so I know straight away whether I did in the last five working days.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but a gate should carry no escape, and here there are two: 'I can't recall one particular job' doesn't fit a yes-or-no about the whole week, and 'I'd rather not say' shouldn't exist at all.
screens.why5: No product leaks, but the founder's moment is a job where memory, GPUs and run time have to be guessed, and 'try to submit a job' drops that guessing and hints at a failed submission instead.
screens.why6: Heard once it's short, one question, and 'Yes or no' is easy to hold.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did you submit a job where you had to set its memory, GPUs and time limit? Yes / No (no escape chip)

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to submitting a job this week, asking how many days I did it is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Plain, but 'try to submit' reads oddly to me because I just submit with sbatch or kubectl, so I pause over whether 'try' means jobs that got rejected or stuck pending.
screens.why3: I know which days this week I submitted runs, so I can answer from memory.
screens.why4: 1 to 5 covers every possible count of working days, the counts don't overlap, and 'I can't recall' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: It stays on the founder's moment of a job being ready to submit, and nothing about a product or tool reaches me.
screens.why6: It's one short question with 'a number from 1 to 5' and the escape said last, so it's easy to answer on one hearing.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, on how many days did you submit a job? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · I can't recall

screens.why1: Right after asking whether and how often I submitted jobs this week, asking which part of it hurt most is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Every option is how I'd talk about cluster work (allocation, getting software working, guessing memory, GPUs and run time, waiting in the queue), though 'last run of jobs' is slightly loose next to the earlier 'submit a job'.
screens.why3: I deal with all five of these myself every time I submit, so I can answer from last week without guessing.
screens.why4: The five are distinct, cover the main pains of a shared cluster, and place the guessing option among equals rather than leading me to it; 'None of these' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: The founder's circumstance appears only as one neutral option among five, with no product or company language reaching me.
screens.why6: It's one short question with five short, parallel options and one escape, so I can hold the list after one hearing.

screens.why1: Right after I picked what I'd most like made easier, asking how sizing my last job actually went is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: The words are mine (memory, GPUs, resubmitted), but 'Think of your last job... before submitting a job go?' says 'job' twice and 'how did guessing go' is clunky, so I read it twice.
screens.why3: I size every job myself and know exactly what happened to my last fine-tuning run.
screens.why4: Each option welds a method to an outcome, so 'sized from past runs but it still got killed' or 'padded a lot and still OOMed' has no home, and 'copied an old script' overlaps with 'sized from past runs' and gives no outcome.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's point, that memory, GPUs and time get guessed up front and either sit idle or kill the job, and no product leaks through.
screens.why6: Spoken, each option is two or three clauses ('padded it a little, it ran, a little idle'), so five of them are hard to hold after one hearing.
screens.instead: Think of your last job. How did the memory, time and GPUs you asked for turn out? About right, it ran fine; too much, a lot sat idle; too little, it was killed partway; or too much, it sat in the queue. Or say you can't recall.

typo_leaks.text: How do researchers get each job to run to the end without wasting the clusterr today?
